THE SAPPHIRE INITIATIVE
BY KEITH LAUMER

It was a simple cultural exchange—but Sebastian Knight gave them more of an education than they expected!

I

Deputy Administrator Michelle Peterson took her embroidered shawl and jade pendant from the wall hook. "I'm off now, Sebastian," she said. "I hope you'll manage the administrative routine during my absence without any unfortunate incidents."

"That seems a modest enough hope," Sebastian said. "I'll try to live up to it."

"I don't appreciate frivolity with reference to this Division," Michelle said testily. "When I first came here, the Cultural Heritage and Environmental Development Directorate was a shambles. I fancy I've made CHED what it is today. Frankly, I question the wisdom of placing you in charge of such a sensitive desk, even for two weeks. But remember. Yours is purely a rubber-stamp function."

"In that case, let's leave it to Ms. Chen. I'll take a couple of weeks off myself. With her experience, she could bring plenty of expertise to bear."

"I assume you jest, Sebastian," Michelle said sadly. "I should expect even you to appreciate that Zenithian participation in the Cultural Exchange Program may be the first step toward sublimation of their industrial aggressions into more sustainable channels."

"I see they're sending three thousand artisans to Greenfield Territory," Sebastian said, glancing at the Memo for Record. "That's a sizable sublimation."

Michelle nodded. "The Zenithians have launched no less than five mining campaigns in the last two decades. They're known as the Strip-Miners of the Proxima Sector. Now, perhaps, we shall see them breaking that precedent and entering into the cultural life of the Coalition."

"Breaking and entering," Sebastian said. "You may have something there. But I'm wondering what they'll study in Greenfield Territory. That's an agricultural world of the poor but honest variety."

"Academic details are the affair of the artisans and their mentors," Michelle said. "Our function is merely to bring them together. See that you don't antagonize the Zenithian representative. This will be an excellent opportunity for you to practice your diplomatic restraint—not your strong point, I'm sure you'll agree."

A buzzer sounded. Sebastian punched a button. "What is it, Ms. Chen?"

"That—rustic person from Parkview is here again." On the small desk screen, Ms. Chen's stern features were compressed in disapproval.

"This fellow's a confounded pest. I'll leave him to you, Sebastian," Michelle said. "Tell him something. Get rid of him. And remember: here at Coalition HQ, all eyes are upon you."

"If I'd thought of that, I'd have worn my other jacket," Sebastian said.

Michelle snorted and passed from view. Sebastian punched Ms. Chen's button.

"Send the rustic person in."

A tall broad woman with sun-darkened skin and silver-streaked hair, wearing practical trousers of heavy canvas, a loose tunic open at the collar and a short vest, stepped into the room. She had a bundle under her arm. She paused at sight of Sebastian, looked him over momentarily, then advanced and held out her hand. Sebastian took it. For a moment the two stood, face to face. The newcomer's jaw muscles knotted. Then she winced.

Sebastian dropped her hand and motioned to a chair.

"That's nice grip work, mister," the stranger said, massaging her hand. "First time anybody ever did that to me. My fault though. I started it, I guess." She grinned and sat down.

"What can I do for you?" Sebastian said.

"You work for this Cultural Heritage bunch, do you? Funny. I thought they were all bureaucrats. Never mind. I'm Isabella Wyatt. I'm a farmer. What I wanted to see you about was—" She shifted in her chair. "Well, out in Parkview, Xandria we've got a serious problem. The sapphire harvest is just about ready. We start gathering in another two, three months. Now I don't know if you're familiar with the Crystal Sapphire plants we cultivate...?"

"No," Sebastian said. "Have a drink?" He pushed a carafe across the desk. Isabella took it. "Crystal Sapphires are an unusual crop," she said, pouring water into a glass. "Only mature every fifteen years. In between, the plants don't need a lot of attention, so our time's mostly our own. We like to farm, though. Spend a lot of time developing new forms. Vegetables the size of a boulder—and delicious—"

"Sounds very pleasant," Sebastian said. "Where does the Cultural Heritage and Environmental Development Division come in?"

Isabella leaned forward. "We go in pretty heavy for the visual arts. Folks can't spend all their time hybridizing plants. We've turned all the land area we've got into parks and farms. Course, we left some sizable forest areas for wildlife preservation and such. Parkview's a nice place, Mr. Knight."

"It sounds like it, Ms. Wyatt. Just what—"

"Call me Isabella. We've got long seasons back home. Six of 'em. Our year's about twenty-two Terra months. Cold as ice in winter; eccentric orbit, you know. Purple-black sky, stars visible all day. We do mostly sculpture and pottery in the winter. Then Spring; still plenty cold. Lots of ice-sailing, snow-trekking, aurora watching; and it's the season for glassworkers. Our crystal work—"

"I've seen some of your crystal work," Sebastian said. "Beautiful pieces."

Isabella nodded. "All local minerals too. Lots of rare earths in our soil and those compounds give the crystals some color, I'll tell you. Then comes the Bloom Season. Flowers—they cover everything. But the sun's getting closer. Shines all the time. Ever seen it with flowers blooming in perpetual daylight? That's the music-composing season. Then summer. Summer's warm. We stay outside most of the time and have community gatherings all night. Lots of open spaces in Parkview; we're mostly valleys and plains. That's the dance and theater time. The stages are set up in the meadows, or on the hillsides. You have the performances and the wildflowers and the bonfires and stars—we're close to the center of a stellar nursery, you know...."

"You say it's time now for the sapphire harvest?"

"That's right. Autumn's our harvest season. Most years we have just the ordinary crops. Grains, tubers, that kind of thing; getting it in doesn't take long. We spend most of the time on architecture, getting new places ready for the winter or renovating the older ones. We spend a lot of time in our dwellings. We like to have them comfortable. But this year's different. This is Sapphire Year."

Isabella sipped her water, looked worriedly at Sebastian. "Our sapphire crop is our big money crop," she said. "We make enough to keep us going. But this year...."

"The crop isn't panning out?"

"Oh, the crop's fine. One of the best I can remember. Course, I'm only thirty-five; I've only worked two harvests myself. The problem's not the crop."

"Have you lost your markets? That sounds like a matter for the Commercial—"

"Lost our markets? Mister, nobody that ever saw our sapphires ever settled for anything else!"

"It sounds like I've been missing something," said Sebastian. "I'll have to see them some time."

Isabella put her bundle on the desk, pulled off the wrappings. "No time like the present," she said.

Sebastian looked at the two crystalline samples, one azure blue, one deep violet, both gleaming with inner light.

"Accepting gifts on duty is frowned on in the Coalition, Ms. Wyatt," he said.

"This isn't a gift. It's just samples." Isabella smiled. "Besides, my feelings would be hurt if you didn't look at them properly." She winked.

Sebastian took a jeweler's loupe from a drawer beside the desk. "Come to think of it, we also have to be careful about violating cultural heritage protocols."

Isabella held up the blue crystal. Sebastian examined it through the loupe, noting the perfect internal structure, then studied it with the naked eye. He looked at Isabella thoughtfully.

"Hmmm. The refraction patterns are extraordinary. Like looking into a living ocean."

"Don't try to describe it, Mr. Knight," Isabella said. She held up the violet crystal. "The custom back home is to view both colors in sequence."

Sebastian examined the second crystal. "Bad luck if you don't appreciate both," Isabella said, nodding. "You probably never heard about the trouble we had in Parkview a few years back?"

"Can't say that I did, Isabella." Sebastian set down the loupe. "Beautiful work."

"We've got plenty of minerals in Parkview," Isabella said. "But we don't plan to wreck the landscape mining 'em. We like to farm and create art. About twelve years back some neighbors of ours landed a force. They figured they knew better what to do with our minerals than we did. Wanted to strip-mine, process ore industrially. We convinced 'em otherwise. But it took a year, and we lost a lot of people."

"That's too bad," Sebastian said. "Environmental justice is a serious matter."

"It put us in a bad spot," Isabella went on. "We had to borrow money from a world called Bayview Territory. Mortgaged our fields. Had to start exporting art work too. Plenty of buyers, but it's not the same when you're doing it for strangers."

"Say, these crystals are remarkable," Sebastian said. "What's the problem? Bayview about to foreclose?"

"Well, the loan's due. The sapphire crop would put us in the clear. But we need harvest hands. Gathering Crystal Sapphires isn't a job you can turn over to machinery—and anyway we wouldn't if we could. Harvest season is the high point of living in Parkview. Everybody joins in. First, there's the gathering in the fields. Miles and miles of crystal gardens covering the valley floors, and climbing the hillsides, with meditation spaces here and there. Tall plants, ten feet high, loaded with crystals, and deep moss growing between. The water-carriers keep on the run, bringing refreshment to the gatherers. There's prizes for the biggest day's output, competitions for who can fill the most baskets in an hour.... The sun's high and bright, and it's just cool enough to give you plenty of energy. Come nightfall, the tables are set up in the garden plots, and the feast is laid on: roasted game, cultivated proteins, grain dishes, all kinds of preparations. Big salads. Plenty of fruit. Fresh-baked bread ... and crystal-clear water from the mountain springs. The cooking's done by a different crew each night in each garden, and there's prizes for the best crews.

"Then the crystal-processing. We still hand-polish each stone. That's mostly for the young folks but anybody's welcome. That's when things start to get creative. Matter of fact, pretty near half our artistic collaborations start after a harvest. All formality is dropped then. It keeps a person inspired though. Ever tried to polish a crystal while working side by side with someone who shares your vision?"

"Never did," Sebastian said. "You say most of the artistic collaborations start after a harvest. That would make the participants only fifteen years old by the time—"

"Oh, that's Parkview years; they'd be twenty-three, Terra reckoning."

"I was thinking you looked a little mature for thirty-five," Sebastian said.

"Fifty-two, Terra years," Isabella said. "Old Marcus, who led the last harvest before the war—he'd worked seven of them. Knew everything there was to know about the crystal gardens. The way the morning dew affects the picking, which sections ripen first in a dry season versus a wet one. He could look at a field and tell you within a day when it would peak."

"Sounds like invaluable knowledge."

Isabella's face clouded. "He didn't make it through the fighting. Neither did most of the other harvest veterans. My mother worked four harvests—she's gone too. My uncle Tobias managed three before he passed." She shook her head slowly. "These days, I'm one of the senior people, and I've only done it twice. The young ones coming up now—they've never worked a sapphire harvest at all. They're eager, sure. Strong backs, willing hands. But there's a thousand things that can go wrong that you only learn by doing."

"What we figured was, maybe you Cultural Heritage people could help us out. A loan to see us through the harvest, enough to hire extra hands. Then we'd repay it in sculpture, paintings, crystal work—"

"Sorry, Isabella. All we do here is work out itineraries for traveling exhibitions, that kind of thing. Now, if you needed a troupe of Andromedan light-dancers—"

"Can they gather crystals?"

"Nope. Anyway, they can't work in daylight. Have you talked this over with the Labor Office?"

"Sure did. They said they'd fix us up with all the digital transformation specialists and climate technology programmers we wanted—but no field hands. Said it was what they classified as menial drudgery; you'd have thought I was trying to buy slaves."

The buzzer sounded. Ms. Chen's features appeared on the desk screen.

"You're due at the Intergroup Council in five minutes," she said. "Then afterwards, there are the Zenithian artisans to meet."

"Thanks." Sebastian stood. "I have to run, Isabella," he said. "Let me think this over. Maybe I can come up with something. Check with me day after tomorrow. And you'd better leave the samples here. Cultural exhibits, you know."

II

As the council meeting broke up, Sebastian caught the eye of a colleague across the table.

"Mr. Hassan, you mentioned a shipment going to a place called Bayview Territory. What are they getting?"

Hassan blinked. "You're the fellow who's filling in for Michelle, over at CHED," he said. "Properly speaking, equipment grants are the sole concern of the Industrial Equipment Distribution, Division of Loans and Exchanges." He pursed his lips. "However, I suppose there's no harm in telling you. They'll be receiving heavy mining equipment."

"Drill rigs, that sort of thing?"

"Strip mining gear." Hassan took a slip of paper from a breast pocket, blinked at it. "Titan Model XV/3 excavators, to be specific. Why is CHED interested in IED's activities?"

"Forgive my curiosity, Mr. Hassan. It's just that Bayview cropped up earlier today. It seems they hold a mortgage on some crystal gardens over in—"

"That's not IED's affair, sir," Hassan cut in. "I have sufficient problems as Chief of IED without probing into CHED's business."

"Speaking of excavators," another person put in, "we over at the Special Committee for Rehabilitation and Development of Under-resourced Nations' Environmental Systems have been trying for months to get a request for mining equipment for Greenfield Territory through IED—"

"SCRUNES was late on the scene," Hassan said. "First come, first served. That's our policy at IED. Good day, colleagues." He strode off, briefcase under his arm.

"That's the trouble with peaceful worlds," the SCRUNES committee member said. "Zenith is a troublemaker, so every agency in the Coalition is out to pacify them. While my chance to make a record—that is, assist peace-loving Greenfield Territory—comes to naught." She shook her head.

"What kind of arts institute do they have in Greenfield Territory?" asked Sebastian. "We're sending them three thousand exchange artisans. It must be quite an institution."

"Arts institute? Greenfield Territory has one under-funded community center."

"Will all the exchange artisans be studying at the Community Center?"

"Three thousand artisans? Hah! Three hundred artisans would overtax the facilities of the center."

"I wonder if the Zenithians know that?"

"The Zenithians? Why, most of Greenfield Territory's difficulties are due to the unwise trade agreement they entered into with Zenith. Three thousand artisans indeed!" She snorted and walked away.

Sebastian stopped by the office to pick up a light jacket, then rode the elevator to the roof of the 180-story Coalition HQ building and hailed a transport to the port. The Zenithian artisans had arrived early. Sebastian saw them lined up on the platform waiting to go through customs. It would be half an hour before they were cleared through. He turned into the lounge and ordered a coffee.

A stocky young person at the next table raised their cup.

"Good fortune," they said.

"And prosperity to match."

"You said it." They gulped half their coffee. "My name's Valentina Evans. Ms. Evans. Yeah, Ms. Evans. This is tedious, sitting around this place waiting...."

"You meeting somebody?"

"Yeah. Bunch of novices. Kids. How they expect—Never mind. Have one on me."

"Thanks. You a mentor?"

"I'll tell you what I am. I'm a shepherd. You know—" Valentina turned to Sebastian—"not one of those kids has more than basic training." She grimaced. "Artisans, you know. Never saw an artisan with real experience, did you?"

"Lots of times. You're meeting the artisans, are you?"

Valentina blinked at Sebastian. "Oh, you know about it, huh?"

"I represent CHED."

Valentina finished her coffee, ordered another. "I came on ahead. Sort of an advance coordinator for the kids. I trained 'em myself. Treated it like a workshop, but they can handle a fabrication unit. Don't know how they'll act under pressure. If I had my old team—"

She looked at her coffee cup, pushed it back. "Had enough," she said. "So long, friend. Or are you coming along?"

Sebastian nodded. "Might as well."

At the exit to the Customs enclosure, Sebastian watched as the first of the Zenithian artisans came through, caught sight of Valentina and straightened up, chest out.

"Drop that, friend," Valentina snapped. "Is that any way for an artisan to act?"

The youth, a lean-faced person with intense eyes, grinned.

"Right, no. Say, uh, Ms. Evans, are we gonna get to see the city? We folks were thinking—"

"You were, hah? You act like a bunch of students! I mean ... no! Now line up!"

"We have quarters ready for the artisans," Sebastian said. "If you'd like to bring them around to the west side, I have a couple of transports arranged."

"Thanks," said Valentina. "They'll stay here until departure time. Can't have the little dears wandering around loose. Might get ideas about going independent." She grimaced. "I mean they might skip orientation."

"We've scheduled your re-embarkation for noon tomorrow. That's a long wait. CHED's arranged gallery visits and a dinner."

"Sorry," Valentina said. "As soon as the equipment gets here, we're off." She grimaced again. "Can't travel without our equipment, y'know."

"Suit yourself," Sebastian said. "Where's the equipment now?"

"Coming in aboard a Bayview lighter."

"Maybe you'd like to arrange for a meal for the artisans here."

"Sure," Valentina said. "That's a good idea. Why don't you join us?" Valentina winked. "And bring some refreshments."

"Not this time," Sebastian said. He watched the artisans, still emerging from Customs. "They seem to be all young adults," he commented. "No senior artisans?"

"Maybe later," Valentina said. "You know, after we see how the first group is received."

Back at the CHED office, Sebastian buzzed Ms. Chen.

"Do you know the name of the institution these Zenithian artisans are bound for?"

"Why, the Arts Institute at Greenfield Territory, of course."

"Would that be the Community Center?"

Ms. Chen's mouth puckered. "I'm sure I've never pried into these details."

"Where does doing your job stop and prying begin, Ms. Chen?" Sebastian said. "Personally, I'm curious as to just what it is these artisans are travelling so far to study—at Coalition expense."

"Ms. Peterson never—"

"For the present, Ms. Chen, Ms. Peterson is on leave. That leaves me with the question of three thousand young artisans headed for a world with no facilities for them ... a world in need of excavators. But the excavators are on their way to Bayview Territory, a world under obligation to Zenith. And Bayview holds a mortgage on the best crystal acreage in Parkview."

"Well!" Ms. Chen snapped, eyes glaring. "I hope you're not questioning Ms. Peterson's wisdom!"

"About Ms. Peterson's wisdom there can be no question," Sebastian said. "But never mind. I'd like you to look up an item for me. How many excavators will Bayview be getting under the IED program?"

"Why, that's entirely IED business," Ms. Chen said. "Ms. Peterson always—"

"I'm sure she did. Let me know about the excavators as soon as you can."

Ms. Chen sniffed and disappeared from the screen. Sebastian left the office, descended thirty-three stories, followed a corridor to the Coalition Library. In the archives he thumbed through catalogues, pored over indices.

"Can I help you?" someone asked. A young librarian stood at his elbow.

"Thank you," Sebastian said. "I'm looking for information on a mining rig. A Titan model XV excavator."

"You won't find it in the industrial section," the librarian said. "Come along." Sebastian followed them along the archives to a well-lit section lettered MILITARY EQUIPMENT. They took a data crystal from the shelf, plugged it into the viewer, scrolled through and stopped at a massive armored vehicle.

"That's the model XV," they said. "It's what is known as a planetary extraction unit. It carries six operators, with devastating environmental impact capability."

"There must be an error somewhere," Sebastian said. "The Titan model I want is an excavator. Model XV M-3—"

"Oh, the modification was the addition of a processing blade for demolition work. That must be what confused you."

"Probably—among other things. Thank you."

Ms. Chen was waiting at the office. "I have the information you wanted," she said. "I've had it for over fifteen minutes. I was under the impression you needed it urgently, and I went to great lengths—"

"Sure," Sebastian said. "Go ahead. How many excavators?"

"Eight hundred."

"Are you sure?"

Ms. Chen's face tightened. "Well! If you feel I'm incompetent—"

"Just questioning the possibility of a mistake, Ms. Chen. Eight hundred excavators is a lot of equipment."

"Was there anything further?" Ms. Chen inquired frigidly.

"I sincerely hope not," Sebastian said.

III

Leaning back in Michelle's ergonomic chair with climate control and posture adjustment, Sebastian leafed through a folder labelled "CERP 9-804-Bt; BAYVIEW TERRITORY (general)." He paused at a page headed Industry.

Still reading, he opened the desk drawer, took out the two crystal samples and examined them in the light. He studied the blue crystal meditatively.

It would be a pity, he reflected, if anything should interfere with the production of such beauty....

Half an hour later he laid the folder aside, keyed the communications panel and put through a call to the Bayview Legation. He asked for the Commercial Attache.

"Knight here, Coalition HQ," he said airily. "About the IED shipment, the excavators. I'm wondering if there's been a mix up. My records show we're shipping eight hundred units...."

"That's correct. Eight hundred."

Sebastian waited.

"Ah ... are you there, Knight?"

"I'm still here. And I'm still wondering about the eight hundred excavators."

"It's perfectly in order. I thought it was all settled. Mr. Hassan—"

"One unit would require a substantial operation to handle its output," Sebastian said. "Now Bayview subsists on its fisheries. They have perhaps half a dozen small processing facilities. Maybe, in a bind, they could handle the ore fifteen XVs could extract ... if Bayview had any ore. It doesn't. By the way, isn't an XV a poor choice as a mining outfit? I should think—"

"See here, Knight! Why all this interest in a few surplus excavators? And in any event, what business is it of yours how we plan to use the equipment? That's an internal affair of my government. Mr. Hassan—"

"I'm not Mr. Hassan. What are you going to do with the other seven hundred and eighty-five excavators?"

"I understood the grant was to be with no strings attached!"

"I know it's bad manners to ask questions. It's an old diplomatic tradition that any time you can get anybody to accept anything as a gift, you've scored points in the game. But if Bayview has some scheme cooking—"

"Nothing like that, Knight. It's a mere business transaction."

"What kind of business do you do with a Titan XV? With or without a blade attached, it's what's known as a planetary extraction unit."

"Great Heavens, Knight! Don't jump to conclusions! Would you have us branded as environmental criminals? Frankly—is this a secure line?"

"Certainly. You may speak freely."

"The excavators are for transshipment. We've gotten ourselves into a difficult situation, balance-of-payments-wise. This is an accommodation to a group with which we have rather strong business ties."

"I understand you hold a mortgage on the best land in Parkview," Sebastian said. "Any connection?"

"Why ... ah ... no. Of course not, ha ha."

"Who gets the excavators eventually?"

"Knight, this is unwarranted interference!"

"Who gets them?"

"They happen to be going to Parkview. But I scarcely see—"

"And who's the friend you're helping out with an unauthorized transshipment of grant material?"

"Why ... ah ... I've been working with a Ms. Oliver Johnson, a Zenithian representative."

"And when will they be shipped?"

"Why, they went out ten days ago. They'll be two-thirds of the way there by now. But look here, Knight, this isn't what you're thinking!"

"How do you know what I'm thinking? I don't know myself." Sebastian rang off, buzzed the secretary.

"Ms. Chen, I'd like to be notified immediately of any new applications that might come in from the Zenithian Consulate for placement of artisans."

"Well, it happens, by coincidence, that I have an application here now. Ms. Johnson of the Consulate brought it in."

"Is Ms. Johnson in the office? I'd like to see her."

"I'll ask if she has time."

"Great. Thanks." It was half a minute before a sharp-featured woman in severe attire walked in. She wore modern styling, a crisp uniform, polished boots and an impatient expression.

"What is it you wish?" she barked. "I understood in my discussions with the other ... ah ... administrator there'd be no further need for these tiresome conferences."

"I've just learned you're placing more artisans abroad, Ms. Johnson. How many this time?"

"Three thousand."

"And where will they be going?"

"Bayview Territory. It's all in the application form I've submitted. Your job is to provide transportation."

"Will there be any other artisans embarking this season?"

"Why ... perhaps. That's Zenith's business." Oliver looked at Sebastian with narrowed eyes. "As a matter of fact, we had in mind dispatching another three thousand to Magnolia, Veldoria."

"Another under-populated world—and in the same sector, I believe," Sebastian said. "Your people must be unusually interested in that region of space."

"If that's all you wanted to know, I'll be on my way. I have matters of importance to see to."

After Oliver left, Sebastian called Ms. Chen in. "I'd like to have a breakdown of all the artisan movements that have been planned under the present program," he said. "And see if you can get a summary of what IED has been shipping lately."

Ms. Chen compressed her lips. "If Ms. Peterson were here, I'm sure she wouldn't dream of interfering in the work of other departments. I ... overheard your conversation with the representative from the Bayview Legation—"

"The lists, Ms. Chen."

"I'm not accustomed," Ms. Chen said, "to intruding in matters outside our responsibility cluster."

"That's worse than listening in on communications, eh? But never mind. I need the information, Ms. Chen."

"Loyalty to my Chief—"

"Loyalty to your position should send you moving for the material I've asked for," Sebastian said. "I'm taking full responsibility. Now go."

The buzzer sounded. Sebastian flipped a key. "CHED, Knight speaking...."

Isabella's weathered face appeared on the desk screen.

"Hello, Sebastian. Okay if I come up?"

"Sure, Isabella. I want to talk to you."

In the office, Isabella took a chair. "Sorry if I'm rushing you, Sebastian," she said. "But have you got anything for me?"

Sebastian gestured at the crystal samples. "What do you know about Bayview Territory?"

"Bayview? Not much of a place. Mostly ocean. All right if you like fish, I guess. We import our seafood from there. Nice shellfish in storm season. Over two pounds each."

"You on good terms with them?"

"Sure, I guess so. Course, they're pretty thick with Zenith."

"So?"

"Didn't I tell you? Zenith was the bunch that tried to take us over here a dozen years back. They'd've made it too, if they hadn't had a lot of bad luck. Their equipment sank in the wetlands, and without equipment they're manageable."

Ms. Chen buzzed. "I have your lists," she said shortly.

"Bring them in, please."

The secretary placed the documents on the desk. Isabella caught her eye and grinned. She sniffed and left the room.

"What that person needs is a joyful time in the crystal gardens," Isabella observed. Sebastian thumbed through the documents, pausing to read from time to time. He finished and looked at Isabella.

"How many people do you need for the harvest, Isabella?" Sebastian inquired.

Isabella examined her crystal sample and looked thoughtful. "That's the tricky part. The harvest requires real judgment—reading the fields, knowing when to pick, coordinating the crews. My grandmother used to say you needed at least five harvests under your belt before you could trust your instincts."

"And how many people in Parkview have that kind of background now?"

Isabella's expression grew pained. "That's just it. After the war... well, the ones who stood against Zenith were mostly the older folks. The ones who'd been through multiple harvests and knew what the land was worth." She paused. "Now there's me with my two harvests, and a handful of others with the same. The twenty-three-year-olds are enthusiastic, sure—they've got energy to spare and they're ready to work dawn to dusk. But when a section starts showing early signs of over-ripening, or when the morning conditions suggest we need to shift our whole approach..." She shook her head. "That's when you need people who've seen it before."

"Two hundred would help," she said finally. "Two thousand would be better. Here's hoping."

"What would you say to three thousand?"

"Three thousand? Sebastian, you're not joking?"

"I hope not." He picked up the communications panel, called the Port Authority, asked for the dispatch coordinator.

"Hello, Zhang. Say, I have a favor to ask of you. You know that contingent of Zenithian artisans. They're traveling aboard the two Coalition transports. I'm interested in the equipment that goes with the artisans. Has it arrived yet? Okay, I'll wait."

Zhang came back to the panel. "Yeah, Sebastian, it's here. Just arrived. But there's a strange thing. It's not consigned to Greenfield Territory. It's ticketed clear through to Parkview."

"Listen, Zhang," Sebastian said. "I want you to go over to the warehouse and take a look at that equipment for me."

Sebastian waited while the dispatch coordinator carried out the errand. He was studying the violet crystal when Zhang returned to the panel.

"Hey, I took a look at that equipment, Sebastian. Something suspicious going on. Weapons. Plasma cutters, Mark IX energy rifles, demolition charges—"

"It's okay, Zhang. Nothing to worry about. Just a mix-up. Now, Zhang, I'm going to ask you to do something more for me. I'm covering for a colleague. It seems they made an error. I wouldn't want word to get out, you understand. I'll send along a written change order in the morning that will cover you officially. Meanwhile, here's what I want you to do...."

Sebastian gave instructions, then rang off and turned to Isabella.

"As soon as I get off a couple of messages, I think we'd better get down to the port, Isabella. I think I'd like to see the artisans off personally."
